content: Famotidine injection is a medication that inhibits gastric acid secretion. It is FDA-approved for treating certain hospitalized patients with pathological hypersecretory conditions, intractable ulcers, and for short-term management of duodenal ulcers and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Common side effects include constipation, diarrhea, dizziness, and headache. Famotidine injection is intended for intravenous use only and is supplied as a concentrated solution. It is indicated for hospitalized patients with pathological hypersecretory conditions or intractable ulcers, or as an alternative to oral forms for patients unable to take oral medication. For active duodenal ulcers, most patients heal within four weeks, and treatment rarely extends beyond six to eight weeks. Maintenance therapy at reduced dosages may be used after healing. For active benign gastric ulcers, most patients heal within six weeks, and safety beyond eight weeks has not been established. For GERD, short-term treatment is indicated. In patients with moderate or severe renal insufficiency, the elimination half-life of famotidine is prolonged, potentially exceeding 20 hours in severe cases. To avoid drug accumulation and central nervous system side effects, the dose may be reduced to half or the dosing interval extended to 36-48 hours based on clinical response. Pediatric patients with renal insufficiency may also require dosage adjustments. For pathological hypersecretory conditions, the recommended adult intravenous dose is 20 mg every 12 hours, with adjustments based on individual needs. Higher doses may be required in some cases, such as severe Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, where oral doses up to 160 mg every six hours have been used. Famotidine injection can be prepared for intravenous infusion by diluting 2 mL of the solution with 100 mL of compatible solutions like 5% dextrose and infusing over 15-30 minutes. Antacids may be used concomitantly if needed. Parenteral drug products should be inspected visually for particulate matter and discoloration before administration. Famotidine injection is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to any of its components or other H2-receptor antagonists. Cross-sensitivity has been observed within this class of drugs. Symptomatic response to famotidine does not rule out the presence of gastric malignancy. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include fever, fatigue, arrhythmias, liver enzyme abnormalities, nausea, vomiting, and rare cases of agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Hypersensitivity reactions such as anaphylaxis and angioedema have been reported. Central nervous system effects, including seizures, hallucinations, and confusion, have been observed, particularly in patients with renal impairment. Rare skin reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis have also been reported. In pediatric patients, famotidine has been studied for GERD and peptic ulcers. However, data are insufficient to establish precise response rates with specific doses and durations. Treatment duration and dosage should be individualized based on clinical response, gastric pH determination, and endoscopy. Famotidine has been used in pediatric patients under one year of age, but its safety and efficacy beyond four weeks have not been established. Famotidine is excreted in breast milk, and its use in nursing mothers should be carefully considered due to potential adverse effects on infants. In pregnant women, famotidine should only be used if clearly needed, as animal studies have not always been predictive of human response. Famotidine injection is supplied as a sterile, concentrated solution for intravenous use. It should be stored at 2° to 8°C (36° to 46°F) and protected from light. Diluted solutions should be refrigerated and used within 48 hours if not administered immediately. Famotidine is a competitive inhibitor of histamine H2-receptors, primarily inhibiting gastric acid secretion. It suppresses both the acid concentration and volume of gastric secretion. After oral administration, the antisecretory effect begins within one hour, with a duration of 10-12 hours for doses of 20-40 mg. Intravenous administration achieves maximum effect within 30 minutes. Famotidine has minimal effects on fasting or postprandial serum gastrin levels and does not affect gastric emptying or exocrine pancreatic function. Famotidine has shown no evidence of carcinogenic potential in long-term animal studies. It was negative in mutagenicity tests and did not impair fertility or reproductive performance in animal studies.
